questions.q: What is the right design question for a small team's environment strategy, per this lesson?
options: How do we build the largest possible number of environments regardless of cost
Which of the course's environments actually earns its cost at this specific size, not how do we get more environments
How do we eliminate all non-production environments entirely
How do we copy an enterprise's full environment setup exactly
questions.explain: A small team shouldn't build a scaled-down copy of enterprise sprawl -- the right question is which environments are actually justified by this team's size and risk profile.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's design give Meridian's two admins separate Developer sandboxes instead of one shared sandbox?
options: Because Salesforce technically forbids more than one admin from sharing a sandbox
Because separate sandboxes are required for any org with more than 10 users
To stop the admins' in-progress work from colliding with each other, applying the isolation principle from Lesson 2
Because shared sandboxes cannot support Flows
questions.explain: Meridian had already experienced two incidents where one person's in-progress changes broke another's work -- exactly the isolation problem a shared development environment creates.

questions.q: What specific risk does Meridian's design knowingly accept by skipping a dedicated staging tier?
options: The risk that a bug which only shows up against full production data volume could reach production undetected
The risk that admins will never be able to log into the org again
The risk that Salesforce will revoke the org's license
There is no risk at all -- skipping staging has no downside at any org size
questions.explain: Without a Full-sandbox staging tier, Meridian can't catch the kind of full-data-volume issue Lesson 6 described (like a batch job hitting governor limits only at real scale) -- a bet this lesson calls defensible at Meridian's size.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's design give the consultant access to the Development sandboxes but not the Testing sandbox?
options: Because the consultant's work is almost always metadata-level and doesn't need to touch even sampled real data, consistent with the least-privilege scoping from Lesson 11
Because Testing sandboxes cannot technically support external logins
Because the consultant already has full production access
Because consultants are never trustworthy enough for any sandbox access
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 11's least-privilege principle -- access should match actual need, and the consultant's metadata-focused work doesn't justify access to the sampled real data in the Testing sandbox.

questions.q: As Meridian grows from 15 to 40 people with its first dedicated QA hire, what does this lesson's framing suggest is the most relevant trigger for revisiting the environment strategy?
options: The team should immediately delete all existing sandboxes and start over
No change is ever needed once an environment strategy is designed
The company should switch Salesforce editions regardless of any other factor

Growth in team size and the addition of a role (QA) that the original design didn't account for is exactly the kind of change that should prompt re-evaluating which risks are still acceptable to accept
questions.explain: This lesson frames the original design's risk acceptance (like skipping staging) as a bet tied to Meridian's current size -- growth and new roles are exactly the kind of change that should prompt revisiting whether that bet still holds.
